4: The dag representation of basic blocks

questions.q: Show the output of each phase of a compiler for the statement position = initial + rate * 60, where all variables are float.
questions.model: Lexical: id1 = id2 + id3 * 60. Syntax: tree with = at the root, + over id2 and (* over id3 and 60). Semantic: inttofloat(60) inserted. Intermediate: t1 = inttofloat(60); t2 = id3 * t1; t3 = id2 + t2; id1 = t3. Optimisation: t1 = id3 * 60.0; id1 = id2 + t1. Code generation: LDF R2, id3; MULF R2, R2, #60.0; LDF R1, id2; ADDF R1, R1, R2; STF id1, R1.

questions.q: Which cousin of the compiler handles #include directives and macro expansion before compilation?
questions.model: The preprocessor processes directives and expands macros.

questions.q: How many tokens does a C lexical analyser produce for the statement: if (x >= 10) y = x * 2;
Explain the two-buffer input scheme with sentinels and why it speeds up lexical analysis.
questions.model: Input is read into two halves alternately; the lexeme-begin and forward pointers move through them. A sentinel (eof) at the end of each half means only one test per character is needed instead of separate end-of-buffer and end-of-file checks.

questions.q: For the grammar E -> TE', E' -> +TE' | e, T -> FT', T' -> *FT' | e, F -> (E) | id, compute FIRST and FOLLOW of every non-terminal and fill the LL(1) table entries for E' and T'.
questions.model: FIRST(E) = FIRST(T) = FIRST(F) = {(, id}; FIRST(E') = {+, e}; FIRST(T') = {*, e}. FOLLOW(E) = FOLLOW(E') = {), $}; FOLLOW(T) = FOLLOW(T') = {+, ), $}; FOLLOW(F) = {*, +, ), $}. M[E', +] = E' -> +TE'; M[E', )] = M[E', $] = E' -> e. M[T', *] = T' -> *FT'; M[T', +] = M[T', )] = M[T', $] = T' -> e.

questions.q: Compare SLR, canonical LR(1) and LALR parsers in terms of the grammars they accept and the size of their parsing tables. Which is used by parser generators such as Yacc, and why?
questions.model: Power: SLR < LALR < LR(1). Table size: SLR and LALR have the same number of states (LR(0) items), LR(1) many more. Yacc/Bison use LALR: nearly the power of LR(1) with SLR-sized tables.

questions.q: True or False: An operator-precedence grammar may contain a production whose right side has two adjacent non-terminals.
questions.model: False. Operator grammars have no e-productions and no two adjacent non-terminals on any right side.

questions.q: Write a Yacc/Bison specification for a calculator that evaluates expressions with integers, +, *, and parentheses, giving * higher precedence than +.

Using the S-attributed definition E -> E1 + T {E.val = E1.val + T.val}, E -> T, T -> T1 * F {T.val = T1.val * F.val}, T -> F, F -> digit {F.val = digit.lexval}, draw the annotated parse tree for 3 * 5 + 4 and give the value at the root.
questions.model: T.val = 3 * 5 = 15 on the left; T for 4 has val 4; E.val = 15 + 4 = 19 at the root. Attributes are computed bottom-up.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about L-attributed definitions and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Every S-attributed definition is also L-attributed.
questions.reason: An S-attributed definition uses only synthesized attributes, which an L-attributed definition always allows.
questions.model: Both true and R explains A.

questions.q: Which storage-allocation strategy is required to support recursive procedures?
questions.model: Each activation needs its own record, pushed and popped on the control stack.

questions.q: Given void f(int a, int b) { a = a + b; b = a + b; } and int x = 1, y = 2; f(x, y); with both parameters passed by reference, what is the value of x + y after the call?
questions.model: a aliases x: x = 1 + 2 = 3; b aliases y: y = 3 + 2 = 5; x + y = 8 (by value it would stay 3).

questions.q: Generate three-address code for a = b * -c + b * -c and represent it as quadruples.
questions.model: t1 = minus c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = minus c; t4 = b * t3; t5 = t2 + t4; a = t5. Quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result): (minus, c, -, t1), (*, b, t1, t2), (minus, c, -, t3), (*, b, t3, t4), (+, t2, t4, t5), (=, t5, -, a).

questions.q: How many basic blocks does this code contain? (1) i = 1 (2) t1 = i * 4 (3) a[t1] = 0 (4) i = i + 1 (5) if i <= 10 goto (2) (6) x = 0
questions.model: Leaders: (1) first statement, (2) jump target, (6) follows a jump. Blocks: {1}, {2-5}, {6}.

questions.t: The dag representation of basic blocks
questions.q: Construct the DAG for the basic block a = b + c; b = a - d; c = b + c; d = a - d, and use it to remove the redundant computation.
questions.model: Nodes: n1 = b0 + c0 (a); n2 = n1 - d0 (b, later also d, since a and d are unchanged); n3 = n2 + c0 (c). Optimised block: a = b + c; b = a - d; c = b + c; d = b.

questions.q: Explain how backpatching generates jumping code for boolean expressions in a single pass, using truelist and falselist.
questions.model: Jumps are emitted with empty targets and their addresses kept in lists (truelist, falselist). When the target becomes known (e.g. the marker before the next statement), backpatch fills it into every jump on the list; merge combines lists for OR and AND.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a peephole optimisation?
opts: Eliminating redundant load and store pairs
Removing unreachable code after an unconditional jump
Algebraic simplification such as x = x + 0
questions.model: Peephole optimisation looks at short windows of target code; global register allocation needs whole-program analysis.

questions.q: Optimise the block t1 = 4 * i; x = a[t1]; t2 = 4 * i; y = a[t2]; t3 = t1; z = t3 + 0 by applying common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, algebraic simplification and dead code elimination. Name each step.
questions.model: CSE: t2 = t1, so y = a[t1]. Copy propagation: z = t1 + 0. Algebraic simplification: z = t1. Dead code: t2 and t3 are no longer used and are removed. Result: t1 = 4 * i; x = a[t1]; y = a[t1]; z = t1.

questions.q: Explain loop-invariant code motion and induction-variable elimination with a short example.
questions.model: Code whose operands do not change in the loop (e.g. t = n * 4 inside for i) is moved to the pre-header. Induction variables change by a constant each iteration (i, and j = 4 * i); j can be updated as j = j + 4 and i removed if only used to compute j.

questions.q: Plan a compiler for the language in the case: describe the phases you would implement, how you would use Flex and Bison, the intermediate representation, and how you would test it.
questions.case: A university wants a small language for writing fee rules, for example: rule late_fee: if days > 10 then amount = 50 + 5 * (days - 10); Rules must be checked for errors and translated into a stack-based bytecode run by the fee system.
questions.model: Flex for tokens (keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators); Bison grammar with precedence for arithmetic and if-then; semantic checks (declared variables, types); generate three-address code, then stack bytecode (push, add, mul, jump-if-false); simple constant folding. Test with unit tests per phase, valid and invalid rule files, and comparison of outputs with hand-computed fees.
